impacts.caseName: Teva Pharmaceuticals International GmbH v. Eli Lilly and Company
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court properly granted judgment as a matter of law that Teva's headache patents claiming methods of using humanized anti-CGRP antagonist antibodies to treat headache were invalid for failure to satisfy the written-description and enablement requirements of 35 U.S.C. § 112.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the district court's JMOL of invalidity, reinstating a jury verdict that Lilly willfully infringed Teva's headache patents covering anti-CGRP antibody treatments. This is a significant ruling in the high-stakes pharmaceutical patent dispute over migraine treatments, directly impacting billions in revenue from blockbuster drugs like Teva's Ajovy and Lilly's competing products.
impacts.positiveImplications: Strengthens patent protection for biologic drug innovators, particularly those claiming genus-level antibody patents with limited species disclosure, making it harder for competitors to invalidate such patents on written-description or enablement grounds.
impacts.negativeImplications: Creates greater exposure for pharmaceutical companies that launch competing biologic products, as willful infringement findings remain intact, potentially leading to enhanced damages and injunctive relief.

impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a patent holder's conditioning of patent licenses on customers' exclusive purchase of the patent holder's unpatented products constitutes unlawful tying under the Sherman Act, even where the patent was found invalid.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed the jury's finding that Ingevity engaged in unlawful tying by conditioning licenses to its fuel-vapor canister patent on customers' exclusive purchase of Ingevity's unpatented carbon honeycomb products. The court upheld the antitrust damages award. This case is significant because it establishes that patent-based tying arrangements can create antitrust liability even for unpatented products that have substantial non-infringing uses.
impacts.positiveImplications: Provides competitors a viable antitrust theory to challenge incumbent patent holders who leverage patent positions to lock in sales of related unpatented products, opening markets to competition.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders who bundle licensing with product purchase requirements face significant antitrust exposure, potentially requiring restructuring of common commercial arrangements that condition patent access on product purchases.

impacts.caseName: The Trustees of Columbia University v. Gen Digital Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether patent claims directed to detecting anomalous program executions by comparing function calls in an emulator to a model are abstract under Alice step one, and whether damages for patent infringement may be based on the patent holder's foreign sales.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated a $185 million jury verdict, holding that Columbia's cybersecurity patents claiming methods for detecting anomalous program executions are abstract at Alice step one and require further proceedings on step two. The court also ruled that damages based on Norton's sales to customers outside the United States were improper, reinforcing territorial limits on patent damages.
impacts.positiveImplications: Provides software and cybersecurity companies with stronger grounds to challenge broadly-worded computer security patents under § 101, and limits patent damages exposure from foreign sales activities.
impacts.negativeImplications: Universities and other patent holders asserting software-related security patents face heightened § 101 vulnerability, and patent holders generally cannot recover damages based on foreign sales, significantly reducing potential awards in cases involving multinational defendants.

impacts.caseName: Global Tubing LLC v. Tenaris Coiled Tubes LLC
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether genuine disputes of material fact precluded summary judgment on both inequitable conduct in obtaining patents and Walker Process antitrust fraud claims based on attempted monopolization.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated summary judgments on both inequitable conduct and Walker Process fraud claims in a dispute over coiled tubing patents, finding genuine disputes of material fact on both issues. The case involves allegations that Tenaris concealed prior art (the CYMAX Documents) from the patent office and used the resulting patents to attempt to monopolize the coiled tubing market.
impacts.positiveImplications: Strengthens the ability of competitors to pursue both inequitable conduct and Walker Process antitrust claims where evidence suggests a patent applicant concealed material prior art, potentially exposing patent holders to treble antitrust damages.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies that acquire prior art through asset purchases face heightened risk that failure to disclose such art during patent prosecution could support both unenforceability and antitrust claims, even when the facts are disputed.

impacts.caseName: GoTV Streaming, LLC v. Netflix, Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether patent claims directed to a server that tailors content presentation specifications to a wireless device's screen size and capabilities are ineligible for patenting under 35 U.S.C. § 101.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit held that GoTV's patents claiming server-side tailoring of content for wireless device capabilities are ineligible under § 101, reversing a jury verdict of infringement and $2.5 million damages award against Netflix. The court found the claims directed to the abstract idea of adapting content presentation to device characteristics.
impacts.positiveImplications: Technology companies defending against patent assertions involving content delivery and device adaptation have stronger § 101 defenses, reducing exposure to patent trolls in the streaming and mobile content space.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders with claims covering server-side content optimization for different devices face significant invalidity risk under § 101, potentially undermining patent portfolios in the content delivery technology sector.

impacts.caseName: Genuine Enabling Technology LLC v. Sony Group Corporation
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the patent holder's failure to account for all elements in the disclosed corresponding structure of a means-plus-function limitation was fatal to its infringement case.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed summary judgment of noninfringement for Sony, holding that GET failed to present a sufficient infringement case because its expert did not account for many elements in the disclosed logic block structure corresponding to a means-plus-function claim limitation. This reinforces the requirement that patentees asserting means-plus-function claims must map all elements of the corresponding structure to the accused product.
impacts.positiveImplications: Provides technology companies like Sony with strong defenses against means-plus-function patent assertions where the patentee fails to perform a thorough structural comparison, lowering litigation costs through early summary judgment.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders asserting means-plus-function claims face a rigorous burden to account for every element in the corresponding structure, making such claims harder to enforce and potentially reducing the value of patents with means-plus-function limitations.

impacts.caseName: VLSI Technology LLC v. Intel Corporation
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a patent holder may recover damages for infringement based on acts occurring entirely outside the United States under the doctrine of equivalents, and whether the district court properly struck damages expert theories for inadequate disclosure.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed in part the district court's summary judgment of noninfringement of VLSI's multicore processor patent against Intel on extraterritoriality grounds, holding that genuine issues of material fact existed. The court affirmed the rejection of VLSI's doctrine of equivalents theory but reversed the striking of VLSI's damages expert theories, remanding for further proceedings.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent holders asserting infringement of semiconductor and processor patents gain a clearer path to recovery where some infringing acts occur domestically, even when accused products are primarily manufactured abroad.
impacts.negativeImplications: Large technology manufacturers like Intel face continued exposure in patent litigation involving multicore processor technology, with the reversal of damages theory exclusions potentially increasing the scope of recoverable damages on remand.

impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a Rule 30(b)(6) corporate representative may testify to matters outside personal knowledge at summary judgment, and whether the on-sale bar under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. § 102(b) requires that prior art sales expressly disclose the functionality of the sold device.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed summary judgment of invalidity under the on-sale bar, holding that Rule 30(b)(6) corporate representatives may testify outside their personal knowledge for summary judgment purposes and rejecting the argument that the on-sale bar requires sales to expressly disclose a device's functionality. This ruling significantly strengthens the on-sale bar defense.
impacts.positiveImplications: Accused infringers can rely on 30(b)(6) testimony from corporate representatives who lack personal knowledge of historical product sales to establish the on-sale bar, making invalidity defenses easier to prove at summary judgment.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders face broader invalidity challenges under the on-sale bar, as prior commercial sales of products embodying claimed inventions need not expressly disclose the patented functionality to trigger the bar.

impacts.caseName: International Medical Devices, Inc. v. Cornell
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the plaintiff established that its asserted trade secrets were protectable under California law, and whether ideas that are generally known can constitute an inventive contribution for patent inventorship purposes.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the trade secret misappropriation verdict, holding there was insufficient evidence that the asserted trade secrets were protectable under California law because the information was generally known. The court also reversed the patent inventorship finding, reasoning that generally known ideas cannot constitute inventive contributions. However, it affirmed the counterfeiting liability verdict.
impacts.positiveImplications: Provides businesses with stronger defenses against trade secret claims where the alleged secrets consist of generally known information, and clarifies that generally known concepts cannot form the basis for inventorship challenges to competitors' patents.
impacts.negativeImplications: Trade secret holders must demonstrate with specificity that their asserted secrets are not generally known in the industry, or risk losing both trade secret protection and the ability to challenge competitors' patents based on the same information.

impacts.caseName: Constellation Designs, LLC v. LG Electronics Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether patent claims directed to non-uniform constellations for digital communications are eligible under 35 U.S.C. § 101, and how to evaluate eligibility for claims that improve upon conventional techniques in a technical field.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the summary judgment of patent eligibility for some asserted patent claims relating to non-uniform constellations used in digital communication systems while affirming eligibility for others, drawing a distinction between claims that recite specific technical implementations and those that do not. The court affirmed infringement and damages findings against LG.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent holders with claims reciting specific technical implementations in communications technology may survive § 101 challenges, and the affirmance of damages provides certainty for licensing in the digital communications standards space.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies implementing communication standards face continued patent infringement risk, and the partial vacatur on eligibility creates uncertainty regarding which types of communications technology claims will survive § 101 scrutiny.

impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a district court abused its discretion by excluding a patent holder's damages expert report and granting summary judgment based on absence of a remedy without permitting supplemental discovery.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the exclusion of Exafer's damages expert report and vacated summary judgment for Microsoft based on absence of a remedy, finding the district court abused its discretion. The ruling reinforces that courts should not exclude damages evidence and then grant summary judgment for lack of damages without affording the patent holder an opportunity to cure deficiencies.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent holders gain protection against procedural traps where courts exclude damages evidence and simultaneously grant summary judgment, ensuring fairer treatment in patent litigation against large technology companies.
impacts.negativeImplications: Accused infringers like Microsoft may face longer and more costly litigation, as courts will be more cautious about granting summary judgment based solely on the exclusion of damages expert testimony.

impacts.caseName: Ascendis Pharma A/S v. BioMarin Pharmaceutical Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether an ITC respondent may obtain a mandatory stay under 28 U.S.C. § 1659(a)(2) of a refiled declaratory judgment action after missing the deadline for a stay in the original action involving the same parties and issues.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit held that an ITC respondent cannot circumvent the mandatory stay deadline under § 1659(a)(2) by voluntarily dismissing a declaratory judgment action and refiling a new one. This prevents gamesmanship in parallel ITC and district court patent proceedings and preserves the statutory deadlines Congress established.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent holders pursuing ITC investigations benefit from the assurance that respondents cannot manipulate district court timelines by strategically dismissing and refiling declaratory judgment actions to obtain mandatory stays they previously forfeited.
impacts.negativeImplications: ITC respondents who miss the 30-day stay deadline lose the ability to obtain mandatory stays of parallel district court proceedings, potentially forcing them to litigate on two fronts simultaneously.

impacts.caseName: 112 Genesee Street, LLC v. United States
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the Restaurant Revitalization Fund statute creates a money-mandating obligation sufficient to confer Tucker Act jurisdiction over claims by restaurant applicants who were denied grants despite applying before later-funded applicants.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed that the RRF statute's directive that the SBA 'shall award grants' in the order applications were received creates a money-mandating obligation conferring Tucker Act jurisdiction. Over 300 restaurants may proceed with claims that they were wrongfully denied pandemic relief grants despite applying before other recipients. This ruling opens the door to significant government liability for misadministration of the $28.6 billion fund.
impacts.positiveImplications: Small businesses and restaurants that applied for but were denied RRF grants have a viable legal path to recover funds, potentially worth millions in aggregate, where the government failed to process applications in the statutorily mandated order.

impacts.caseName: National Veterans Legal Services Program v. United States
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court properly approved a $125 million class action settlement of claims that the federal judiciary overcharged PACER users by using fees to fund expenses unrelated to PACER operations.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed approval of a $125 million nationwide class action settlement resolving claims that the federal judiciary improperly used PACER fees to fund unrelated expenses. The court upheld the settlement, attorneys' fees, and incentive awards to class representatives, finding the settlement fair and adequate given the litigation risks and the comprehensive reimbursement it provided to hundreds of thousands of PACER users.
impacts.positiveImplications: Businesses, law firms, and other frequent PACER users will receive substantial reimbursement of excessive fees paid during the eight-year class period, and the ruling validates the use of incentive awards in class settlements.

impacts.caseName: Willis Electric Co., Ltd. v. Polygroup Ltd. (Macao Commercial Offshore)
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court properly denied JMOL of obviousness and a new trial on damages for a patent covering pre-lit artificial trees with integrated mechanical and electrical connections.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed the denial of Polygroup's motions for JMOL of obviousness and a new trial on damages, upholding a jury verdict that Willis's patent on pre-lit artificial tree technology with simultaneous mechanical and electrical connections was not obvious. This protects a commercially significant patent in the consumer products space.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent holders in consumer products benefit from the court's deference to jury findings on obviousness, supporting enforcement of patents covering commercially successful innovations even where individual components may be found in the prior art.
impacts.negativeImplications: Competitors in the pre-lit artificial tree market remain subject to patent enforcement, potentially limiting product design options and requiring licensing arrangements.
